Which O-Ring Material Do I Need?
Each compound has a distinct chemical compatibility profile and temperature ceiling. Name the medium, the operating temperature and the pressure class, and we will tell you which to specify.
Ethylene acrylic elastomer. Holds compression-set stability where oil, heat and ozone act together.
Fluorocarbon rubber, the first choice for aggressive chemical environments. Resists petroleum oils, fuels and many solvents at sustained high temperature.
Nitrile butadiene rubber, the general-purpose industry standard. Outstanding resistance to petroleum oils and hydraulic fluids at moderate temperature.
Ethylene propylene diene rubber, the preferred material for water, steam and brake fluid service, with excellent weather and ozone resistance. Not for petroleum oils.
Vinyl methyl silicone, the widest service range of the eight. Biocompatible grades available. Poor abrasion resistance — not a wear part.
Polychloroprene. Balanced properties across weather, refrigerants and moderate oil exposure, and the family we reach for when flame retardancy is specified.
Styrene butadiene rubber. Abrasion resistance at low cost, for static seals in water and mild service. Not for oil or fuel contact.
Polyisoprene. The highest resilience of the eight, specified where a seal also has to damp. Not for oil, fuel or sustained heat.
A PTFE jacket over an FKM or silicone core — the chemical resistance of PTFE with the recovery of an elastomer. Specified where a compound would be attacked but a rigid seal cannot follow the groove.
